modern_lens_framing: The Qurʾan is taken here as fixed, revealed truth; science is our provisional, evolving account of the observable world. What follows notes where the two meet — a contemplation, not a proof. Where the science later shifts, that reflects the limits of our knowledge, not the text.

105:5.title: Like Eaten Straw
105:5.in_short: The verse says Allah left Abrahah's army looking like crop-stalks that animals have already eaten and scattered, a picture of total, physical destruction.

claims.text: The whole verse is a simile: the stone-struck army, torn apart and scattered, is compared to the remains of a crop-plant after animals have eaten it, whether that is read as straw, dried leaves, or husk. Several commentators state this as the overall sense of the image.

Other tribes concluded Quraysh were men of God and custodians of His Sacred House, which gave Quraysh safe passage on their trading journeys where other caravans faced raiders.

Rebar's commentary notes that not everyone in the army was destroyed; some fled and survived so that word of what happened could reach their own people as a lesson (ʿibrah), and poses this as a challenge: the people of Makkah saw this with their own eyes, so why do they still not believe in the Prophet ﷺ.

105:5.essay_html:
The verse closes the story of Abrahah's army with a single, stark image: they were left like crop-stalks already eaten. Every commentator treats this as a picture of total, physical destruction, the bodies torn apart and scattered exactly as the leftover parts of a grazed crop are scattered.1,2,3,4,9,13,8,11,12,14

The word for that leftover matter is عصف (ʿaṣf), and the early commentators do not all mean quite the same thing by it. One line, going back to Mujāhid and Qatādah, takes it as the leaves or straw of the wheat plant, left in the field after harvest.1,2,4,7 Ibn ʿAbbās instead reads it as the husk that wraps a grain of wheat, the outer shell that falls away from it.1,2,3,4 ʿIkrimah is reported to have taken it as a grain that has already been eaten out, left hollow.2 Ibn Zayd reads it as the leaves of crops and greens which, once eaten by cattle, come out again as dung, dry, and break into pieces, the very picture given of the bodies here.1,3,4

Al-Qurṭubī (d. 1273 CE) draws out two grammatical points. The particle "like" (كـ) here works exactly as it does in the phrase "nothing is like Him", it marks a comparison, not an equation.3 And "eaten" (مأكول, maʾkūl) is short for "its grain has been eaten", the same kind of shorthand as calling someone "handsome" when strictly it is his face that is handsome. He backs the reading of ʿaṣf as crop-leaves with lines of older Arabic poetry.3

Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373 CE) records that the destruction did not fall on everyone at the same instant. Some died on the spot; others broke apart limb by limb as they tried to flee. Abrahah himself is said to have disintegrated piece by piece on the road, dying only once he reached Ṣanʿāʾ, his heart falling out at the very end.4

Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads the verse as a plain sensory picture, bodies literally crushed and scattered, and says there is no need to reach for theories that smallpox or measles explains the disintegration; the stones alone account for it.6 He also argues that Allah did not let the defence of His House be credited to its polytheist custodians, so that no historical role in protecting the Kaʿbah could ever be claimed for shirk or tribal pride.6

Several commentators draw out what followed. Al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) notes the event fell in the very year the Prophet ﷺ was born, one of the preliminary signs before his mission.5 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976 CE) notes it raised Quraysh's standing across Arabia, other tribes took them for men of God and guardians of His House, which gave their caravans safe passage where others faced raiders.7 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) reads the whole episode as a sign that whoever set himself against the Prophet ﷺ or his mission would meet the same fate.10 Rebar's commentary adds that some of the army fled and survived, so word of what happened could reach their people as a lesson, and asks why the people of Makkah, who saw this with their own eyes, still would not believe.14

Ibn Kathīr also ties the story forward into the Prophet's ﷺ own life. When his she-camel knelt at al-Ḥudaybiyyah and would not rise, he said she had been "stopped by He Who restrained the Elephant", a report carried by al-Bukhārī alone.4 And at the conquest of Makkah he is reported, in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, to have said that Allah had restrained the Elephant from Makkah and given authority over it to him and the believers.4

Whether ʿaṣf is read as straw, husk, or crop-leaf, every reading points the same way: what stone and wind leave of a grazed field is what the stones from the sky left of Abrahah's army.

105:1.title: The Army of the Elephant Foiled
105:1.in_short: The verses recall a famous historical event: an army from Yemen brought elephants to destroy the Kaaba, and the Qur'an reminds the hearer that Allah made their whole scheme come to nothing before it succeeded.

claims.text: The opening words 'Have you not seen' are a rhetorical question used to affirm a known fact (taqrīr), not to ask a real question.

sources.original_excerpt: واللفظ استفهام، والمعنى تقرير
الاستفهام ... للتقرير
এখানে জিজ্ঞাসা সাব্যস্তের জন্য ব্যবহার হয়েছে

claims.text: al-Ṭabarī reads 'seeing' here as looking with the eye of the heart: an inward, certain awareness given to the Prophet ﷺ, not literal eyesight.

sources.original_excerpt: ألم تنظر يا محمد بعين قلبك، فترى بها

original_terms.gloss: with the eye of the heart, inward certainty

claims.text: Because the event happened before or around the Prophet's ﷺ birth, he could not have witnessed it with his own eyes; 'seeing' here means knowledge so firmly established by widespread report that it counts as if seen.

sources.original_excerpt: المراد بالرؤية هنا: العلم المحقق
ألَم تَرَ এর অর্থ হল ألَم تَعلَم

claims.text: Though grammatically addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, the address is general, taking in everyone of that time who knew the famous story, not the Prophet ﷺ alone.

sources.original_excerpt: والخطاب للنبي صلى الله عليه وسلم؛ ولكنه عام

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the question form as expressing wonder at an extraordinary event full of meaning; it was so well known among the Arabs that they dated other events by it, calling it 'the Year of the Elephant'.

sources.original_excerpt: یہ سوالیہ انداز تعجب انگیزی کے لئے اختیار کیا گیا ہے

claims.text: 'The People of the Elephant' refers to the Abyssinian-led army under Abraha that marched on Mecca bringing elephants, intending to demolish the Kaaba.

The background: Abraha built a grand church at Ṣanʿāʾ hoping to turn Arab pilgrimage away from the Kaaba toward it; when someone from Quraysh or Kinānah defiled it (in another report, a fire set by young Quraysh men burned it), Abraha swore to destroy the Kaaba in retaliation.
On the way, Abraha's men seized livestock near Mecca, including two hundred camels belonging to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather, who then went to negotiate with Abraha.
ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib asked Abraha only for the return of his own camels, not for the Kaaba, saying: 'I am the lord of the camels; this House has its own Lord who will defend it.'

sources.original_excerpt: أنا رب هذه الإبل وإن لهذا البيت ربا سيمنعه

claims.text: As the army advanced, the lead elephant (named Maḥmūd) knelt and refused to move toward the Kaaba, though it would walk readily when turned in any other direction; this is linked to Nufayl bin Ḥabīb's words to the animal.
Commentators differ on the number of elephants: Muqātil says there was one; al-Ḍaḥḥāk says eight; another report says twelve besides the great one.

al-Baghawī explains why the Qur'an uses the singular 'the elephant' despite there being several: either because the whole army is named after its single greatest elephant, or for the sake of matching the rhyme-ending of the verses.

sources.original_excerpt: وإنما وحد لأنه نسبهم إلى الفيل الأعظم. وقيل: لوفاق رءوس الآي

claims.text: Scholars differ on when the Year of the Elephant occurred relative to the Prophet's ﷺ birth: forty years before (Muqātil), twenty-three years before (al-Kalbī), while most say it was the very year of his birth.

Because it happened just before his prophetic mission, scholars of Hadith class this event not as a full 'mu'jizah' (a miracle shown to prove a prophet's claim after that claim is made) but as an 'irhāṣ', a preparatory sign preceding it.

original_terms.gloss: a preparatory sign before a prophet's mission begins

claims.text: Physical traces of the event were said to remain visible even after the Prophet's ﷺ birth: two of the elephant's handlers reportedly survived, blind and disabled, begging in Mecca, and were seen by ʿĀ'ishah and Asmāʾ رضي الله عنهما.

report.graded_by: not explicitly graded in the sources; relayed as narration

claims.text: The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have later invoked this history himself, saying at the conquest of Mecca: 'Allah restrained the elephant from Mecca and gave authority over it to His Messenger and the believers, and its sanctity has returned as it was before.'

sources.original_excerpt: إِنَّ اللهَ حَبَسَ عَنْ مَكَّةَ الْفِيلَ، وَسَلَّطَ عَلَيْهَا رَسُولَهُ وَالْمُؤْمِنِينَ

report.graded_by: recorded in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, per Ibn Kathīr

claims.text: Isrār Aḥmad holds that Abraha's campaign had a wider aim than demolishing the Kaaba alone: it also sought to spread Christianity in Arabia and gain control of the trade route running between the eastern lands and Byzantine territory.

sources.original_excerpt: عرب میں عیسائیت پھیلانا اور اس تجارت پر قبضہ کرنا بھی تھا

claims.text: Wahiduddin Khan reads the whole episode as a sign that whoever set himself against the Prophet ﷺ or his mission would be defeated as Abraha's army was, and as Allah's way of showing that the Prophet's cause carried divine backing and that the revelation given to him would be preserved.
'Kaydahum' (their plot) refers to their scheming and effort aimed at destroying the Kaaba.

sources.original_excerpt: يعني مكرهم وسعيهم في تخريب الكعبة

original_terms.gloss: plot, scheme, hidden effort to harm

claims.text: 'Tadlīl' means making their plot come to nothing: wasted, void, and ineffective, so it never reached the goal they intended; Muqātil is reported as glossing it also as loss (khasārah) or nullification (buṭlān).

sources.original_excerpt: في تضليلهم عما أرادوا وحاولوا من تخريبها
قال مقاتل: في خسارة، وقيل: في بطلان
أى: في تخسير وإبطال وتضييع
ألم يجعل ما دبَّروه من شر في إبطال وتضييع

original_terms.gloss: leading astray, here meaning rendering a scheme useless and lost

claims.text: Ṭanṭāwī notes that although Abraha's men came openly to destroy the Kaaba, the Qur'an still calls their effort 'kayd' (covert scheming), because they concealed a deeper malice and enmity toward the people of Mecca greater than what they showed outwardly.

sources.original_excerpt: لأنهم كانوا يضمرون من الحقد والحسد والعداوة لأهل مكة، أكثر مما كانوا يظهرونه

claims.text: al-Saʿdī summarises: Allah sufficed the believers against the enemy's evil and turned their scheming back upon them.

sources.original_excerpt: كفى الله شرهم، ورد كيدهم في نحورهم

claims.text: Sayyid Quṭb reads the second rhetorical question as also affirming (expecting an answer 'yes'), and as a reminder to Quraysh that just as Allah defended His House when they themselves were powerless to defend it, He is equally able to protect the small community of believers whom Quraysh, in their pride, wished to crush.

Isrār Aḥmad reiterates that Abraha's whole scheme, not only the plan to demolish the Kaaba but also his wider aims of spreading Christianity and taking Arab trade routes, was made useless and ineffective.

sources.original_excerpt: کیا اس نے ان کی تمام تدبیروں کو بےکار اور غیر موثر نہیں کردیا

105:1.essay_html:
The verses open with a question: has the Prophet ﷺ not seen how his Lord dealt with the People of the Elephant? Commentators explain that this is not a real question but a rhetorical one, meant to affirm a well-known fact.3,9,11,12 al-Ṭabarī reads the 'seeing' as an inward, certain awareness, a looking with the eye of the heart.1 Others point out that the event happened before or around the Prophet's ﷺ own birth, so he could not literally have watched it, meaning 'seeing' here stands for knowledge so firmly established by widespread report that it counts as if seen.7,9,11,12 Though the words are addressed to him, the sense reaches everyone of that generation who knew the story.3,11 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966 CE) reads the question as expressing wonder at an extraordinary event, so famous that Arabs dated other happenings by it, calling it 'the Year of the Elephant'.6

The story behind the verse is told at length by the historians among the commentators. Abraha, ruling Yemen for Abyssinia, built a grand church at Ṣanʿāʾ, hoping to turn Arab pilgrimage away from the Kaaba toward it. When it was defiled, or in another account burned by a fire lit by young men of Quraysh, Abraha swore to march on Mecca and pull the Kaaba down stone by stone.1,2,3,4,7,12,14 On the way his troops seized livestock near Mecca, including two hundred camels belonging to ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, the Prophet's ﷺ grandfather.1,2,3,4,7,12,14 When ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib went to Abraha, he asked only for his camels back, saying: 'I am the lord of the camels; this House has its own Lord who will defend it.'1,2,3,4,7,12,14 As the army turned toward the Kaaba, its lead elephant, named Maḥmūd, knelt and would go no further, though it walked readily when turned any other way.1,2,3,4,7,10,12,14

Details differ in the reports. Some say there was a single elephant, others eight, others twelve besides the great one.1,2,3 al-Baghawī (d. 1122 CE) explains the Qur'an's singular 'the elephant' as naming the whole army after its greatest beast, or simply to match the rhyme of the verse-endings.2 On timing, some say the event was forty years before the Prophet's ﷺ birth, some twenty-three, though most hold it was the very year he was born.2,3,7,10,11,12 Because it came just before his mission, scholars of Hadith class it not as a full miracle proving a prophetic claim but as an 'irhāṣ' — a preparatory sign going before it.7 Traces were said to remain visible afterward: two of the elephant's handlers reportedly survived, blind and disabled, begging in Mecca, and were seen by ʿĀ'ishah and Asmāʾ رضي الله عنهما.3,4,7,11 The Prophet ﷺ himself is reported to have recalled the episode at the conquest of Mecca, saying that Allah had restrained the elephant from the city and given authority over it to him and the believers.4 Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010 CE) adds that Abraha's aims went beyond the Kaaba, to spreading Christianity and controlling the trade route between east and Byzantium.8 Wahiduddin Khan (d. 2021 CE) takes the whole event as a sign that whoever opposed the Prophet ﷺ or his mission would be defeated just as Abraha's army was.10

The second verse turns to the outcome: did Allah not make their plot (kayd, scheming aimed at harm) go astray (taḍlīl)? The commentators gloss 'their plot' as their planning and effort to tear down the Kaaba.1,2,9 'Taḍlīl' is explained as making that plot come to nothing — wasted, void, never reaching what it aimed at; Muqātil is reported to have glossed it also as loss or nullification.1,2,3,9,13 Ṭanṭāwī (d. 2010 CE) observes that though Abraha's men marched openly, the Qur'an still calls their effort 'kayd', because behind the open march lay a hidden malice and enmity toward the people of Mecca greater than what they showed.9 al-Saʿdī (d. 1957 CE) sums up the outcome plainly: Allah sufficed the believers against the enemy's evil and turned their own scheming back upon them.5 Sayyid Quṭb reads the question as a reminder to Quraysh: the same power that defended the House when they themselves were helpless to defend it is equally able to protect the small community of believers whom Quraysh, in their pride, wished to crush.6 Isrār Aḥmad closes the circle: not only the plan to destroy the Kaaba but Abraha's wider ambitions were made useless.8

What the sources agree on is the shape of the lesson: an army came with overwhelming force and a clear plan against the House of Allah, and that plan was turned to nothing before it ever succeeded.1,2,3,5,9,13

105:3.title: The Birds and the Stones
105:3.in_short: Allah sent flocks of birds against Abraha's army, each carrying small baked-clay stones, which struck the soldiers and destroyed them.

claims.text: Ababil means flocks or groups of birds arriving one after another or from every direction. It is not the name of a specific species of bird.

original_terms.gloss: flocks or groups of birds, coming in succession or from all sides

claims.text: Grammarians disagreed over whether Ababil has a singular form at all. Some said it has none; others proposed forms such as ibala, ubul, or abil, though none of these was confirmed as widely known Arabic usage.

original_terms.gloss: proposed but unconfirmed singular forms of Ababil

claims.text: Early exegetes described the birds physically in different ways: with beaks like birds but paws like dogs (Ibn ʿAbbas); green, with heads like predators, coming out of the sea (ʿIkrimah); black sea-birds carrying stones in their beaks and claws (Muhammad b. Kaʿb, ʿUbayd b. ʿUmayr); white birds; green birds with yellow beaks (Saʿid b. Jubayr); resembling swallows (ʿAʾishah) or bats. Ibn Kathir notes the chains for several of these reports are sound.

report.graded_by: Ibn Kathīr calls several of the chains sound (ṣaḥīḥ) but the full set is left ungraded here

claims.text: A report reaching back to the Prophet ﷺ, through Ibn ʿAbbas, describes these birds as flying between heaven and earth, nesting and hatching there.
Each bird carried three stones, one in its beak and one in each claw, and pelted the enemy with them.
The stones were small, described as between the size of a lentil and a chickpea.
Sijjil is explained as an Arabised Persian compound of sang (stone) and gil (clay): a stone made of hardened, baked clay.

original_terms.gloss: hardened, baked clay stone, from Persian sang (stone) + gil (clay)

claims.text: Some scholars read Sijjil as linked to sijill, a written record: the stones came from a decree already written against these people, just as their deeds were recorded in a register.

Ibn Zayd held that Sijjil is a name for the lowest heaven, the same heaven from which stones were sent down on the people of Lut. al-Tabari rejects this view, saying he knows no sound basis for it in report, reason, or language.

The stones struck with great force, piercing bodies through, entering at the head and exiting from below, or entering one side and exiting the other. A fierce wind that Allah sent alongside the birds is said to have increased the force of the stones.
Being struck by the stones caused pustules resembling smallpox, and it is said this was the first time smallpox was seen in the land of the Arabs.

Sayyid Qutb argues there is no need to explain the men's destruction through natural processes like smallpox or measles. The Qur'an's own image, of bodies reduced like chewed-up straw, already says the stones themselves crushed them.
Not everyone was struck at once. Some in the army died immediately, while others, including Abraha himself, suffered a gradual bodily disintegration as they fled.
Isrār Aḥmad observes that Allah needed no extraordinary means to destroy Abraha's vast army: small birds arriving from the coast, and a few moments of stone-throwing, were enough to wipe it out.
The pebbles themselves were unremarkable, small clay stones without any inherent destructive power. It was Allah who gave them a devastating force, greater than a bullet or cannon-shot.

Wahiduddin Khan situates the episode historically: Abraha, a sixth-century Christian ruler of Yemen, marched on Makka in the year of the Prophet's birth with about sixty thousand men and a dozen elephants. As they neared Makka the elephants refused to advance, then flocks of birds dropped pebbles on the army, afflicting it with a strange disease that put it to flight, killing Abraha and many of his men on the way home.

The common recitation reads tarmīhim ("she/it pelts them", the birds), but another reading has yarmīhim ("he pelts them"), taken to refer to Allah directly, comparable to the phrasing "but Allah threw" elsewhere in the Qur'an.

original_terms.gloss: she/it pelts them (referring to birds) / he pelts them (referring to Allah), two reported recitations

105:3.essay_html:
These two verses describe the strike itself. Allah sent flocks of birds against Abraha's army, and those birds pelted them with small stones of baked clay.

The word Ababil describes flocks or groups of birds coming one after another or from every side. It is not the name of a species.1,2,3,4,5,6,7,9,11,12,13,14 Grammarians even argued over whether the word has a singular at all. Some proposed forms like ibala or ubul, but none of these was firmly established as ordinary Arabic.1,2,3,4

Exegetes did not agree on what the birds looked like. Reports describe them with dog-like paws and bird-like beaks, or green with heads like predators, or black sea-birds carrying stones, or white, or resembling swallows or bats.1,2,3,4 Ibn Kathīr (d. 1373) notes that several of the chains behind these descriptions are sound, though the reports themselves differ widely. One further report, going back to the Prophet ﷺ through Ibn ʿAbbas, has him describing these birds as living between heaven and earth, nesting and hatching there.3

Each bird is said to have carried three stones, one in its beak and one in each claw, and to have hurled them at the army.1,2,4,8,9 The stones themselves were small, somewhere between a lentil and a chickpea in size.1,3,4 Yet their effect was devastating: reports describe a stone entering at a man's head and coming out below, and a fierce wind sent alongside the birds is said to have driven the stones with even greater force.2,4,9 Being struck is also said to have raised sores resembling smallpox, the first such outbreak seen in Arab lands.1,3,9 Sayyid Quṭb (d. 1966) pushes back against reading the destruction as simply a disease like smallpox or measles. The Qur'an's own image of the men afterwards, like straw that has been eaten and crushed, already tells the reader that the stones themselves did the work.6 Not everyone was struck at the same moment. Ibn Kathīr relays that some died on the spot, while others, including Abraha himself, fell apart gradually as they tried to flee.4

Sijjil, the word used for the stones, is generally explained as an Arabised Persian compound, sang (stone) and gil (clay), meaning a stone of hardened, baked clay.1,4,6,7,8,9,11,12,13 Others connect it to sijill, a written record, as if the stones carried out a punishment already decreed and written down.3,9 Ibn Zayd went further, holding that Sijjil names the lowest heaven itself, the same heaven from which stones fell on the people of Lūṭ. al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) rejects this, saying he finds no sound support for it in report, reason, or language.1 A minor point of recitation is also noted: most read tarmīhim ("it pelts them", the birds), though another reading has yarmīhim ("He pelts them"), taken to point to Allah as the true actor behind the birds' throw.3

Two commentators draw out what the scene says about power. Isrār Aḥmad (d. 2010) observes that Allah needed nothing extraordinary to break a great army: ordinary birds from the coast and a few moments of stone-throwing were enough.8 Muftī Muḥammad Shafīʿ (d. 1976), together with Zakariyyā and Ahsanul Bayān, makes a related point: the pebbles were unremarkable clay stones with no destructive power of their own, until Allah gave them a force greater than any bullet or cannon-shot.7,11,12

Small birds, small stones, and by the sources' account, a mighty army left as though it had never stood.
